gold_decisions.identity_explanation: The gold issue concerns reversing the flow and applying the wrong map in the executable sampling instruction, whereas ISSUE-001 concerns the mismatch between standard Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature and integration against a nonuniform measure. They involve different mathematical objects and failed operations; the shared presence of an integration-related construction is not substantive overlap.

The gold issue is the unsupported uniform smoothness and resulting class-uniform approximation bounds over target densities with unrestricted C^k norms. ISSUE-002 instead diagnoses a quantifier error coupling the quadrature budget to sample size. It does not recognize the missing target-class regularity assumption or the failure of uniform model bounds.

The gold issue concerns comparing Jacobians evaluated at different inverse-flow points and omitting the spatial Lipschitz/displacement term. ISSUE-001 concerns quadrature weights and the underlying integration measure. It provides no diagnosis of the missing change-of-point estimate in the flow-Jacobian comparison.

The gold issue is the invalid uniform conversion from determinant differences to log-determinant differences near zero and the missing reciprocal lower-bound factor. ISSUE-001 diagnoses an incorrectly weighted quadrature rule, not a log-Jacobian sensitivity estimate, so it does not recognize the relevant formula or conditioning obligation.

ISSUE-002 explicitly identifies that the quadrature error budget depends on n, so setting a fixed m threshold at the sample threshold does not establish the theorem for every larger n. It states the resulting coupled condition m≥m(n), exactly matching the gold defect in the independent n and m quantifiers.
gold_decisions.shared_mathematical_weakness: Both identify the failure to prove a quadrature threshold independent of sample size: the error prefactor can grow with n, so a fixed m chosen from n* need not control all n≥n*.

component_coverage.gold_component: The quadrature estimate yields an n-dependent sufficient budget m(n), and no argument shows that the budget at n* controls all larger n.
